title: Mark
subtitle: All Sixteen Chapters - Key Notes, Cross-References, and Prophecy Fulfilled (WEB)

items.value: This book walks through all sixteen chapters of Mark, one chapter at a time, with the full text of every chapter printed in it. It grew out of a series of study guides written for a group working through Mark three chapters a week, and it is the fourth volume in this series.

Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels and the fastest. It has no genealogy, no birth narrative, and almost no long discourse. It opens at full speed and does not slow down. Read it in one sitting and the effect is deliberate - you are meant to feel hurried, and to arrive at the cross slightly out of breath.
It is a companion to the Jeremiah, Matthew and Malachi volumes in this series, and it is built the same way. If you have used any of those, everything here will be familiar.

The prose is the point. The tables and footnotes are apparatus - useful, and worth using - but they exist to serve a reading of Mark, not to replace one. If you only ever read the chapter introductions and the scripture text, you will have read this book properly.

sections.heading: How this book is put together

items.value: Every chapter follows the same shape.

values: **Key Notes** - the observations worth having in hand before you read: a word that carries more than the translation shows, a custom the first readers took for granted, a connection to something earlier in the book. Each note ends with the verses it comes from.
**Key Cross-References** - eight passages that stand behind or alongside the chapter, grouped by theme.
**Prophecy Fulfilled** - six or seven places where the chapter runs back into the Hebrew Scriptures. The heading is shared with the Matthew volume, and there is a caveat about it below.
**For Further Study** - three places to go deeper, from three different traditions.
**Introduction** - the chapter read as a whole before you read it in parts.
**The chapter itself**, printed in full in the World English Bible, with footnote markers on the verses the references belong to.

items.value: Every scripture reference in the book is a live link to the World English Bible on BibleGateway. In the interactive edition, hovering over a footnote marker shows the full text of the passages cited and a line on why they connect, so you can follow a cross-reference without losing your place.

sections.heading: A note on the second table

items.value: The second table in each chapter is headed **Prophecy Fulfilled**, the same as in the Matthew volume, so that anyone reading both Gospels is not relearning the apparatus halfway through.

But it is worth being straight about a difference. Matthew earns that heading: he uses an explicit formula - "this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet" - about a dozen times, and the argument of his Gospel is built on it. Mark does that once, in the opening lines, and then essentially stops.

Mark writes for readers who do not know the Hebrew Scriptures well. He translates Aramaic when he uses it and explains Jewish custom when it matters, which Matthew never bothers to do. So in this volume the table is doing something slightly different: it is showing the Scriptures that stand behind the action, whether or not Mark pauses to point at them. Often he does not point, and the connection is the stronger for being assumed.

sections.heading: A note on the divine names

items.value: In the notes and introductions this book uses **Yahweh** for the covenant name of God and **Yahshua** for the Messiah, as the group this material was written for does.

The printed scripture text is never altered. The World English Bible reads Jesus in the Gospels, and it stands exactly as the translators set it. So you will see Yahshua in a paragraph of commentary and Jesus in the verse beneath it. That is deliberate, and it is not a claim that one is a better translation of the Greek. It simply keeps our own speech and the translator's work visibly distinct.

sections.heading: A note on the chapter titles

items.value: The chapter titles in this book are not traditional and are not found in any Bible. They were written for this study - they name what struck us in that chapter rather than summarising it. Nobody should take them as headings the text itself supplies.

sections.heading: A note on how Mark ends

items.value: This book prints Mark 16:1-20 in full, as the World English Bible does. But you should know what you are reading, because the last twelve verses are the most disputed passage in the New Testament.

The two oldest complete Greek manuscripts of Mark - Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century - end the Gospel at 16:8, with the women fleeing the tomb and saying nothing to anyone. Several early writers who quote Mark heavily appear not to know verses 9 to 20. Other manuscripts carry a shorter alternative ending instead, and some carry both. Set against that, the longer ending is present in the overwhelming majority of manuscripts, it was known by the second century, and the church has read it as Scripture for a very long time.

This book takes no position on which reading is original. What it does do is tell you where the question lies, and where the evidence sits on each side, rather than printing twelve verses as though nothing were at stake.

One practical word. Verses 17 and 18 mention taking up serpents and drinking deadly things. Whatever you conclude about the passage, these are descriptions of what accompanied the apostolic mission, not instructions to test God - and the one time anyone in the New Testament handles a snake, it is by accident. People have died taking that text as a command. Do not.

sections.heading: Who wrote it, and for whom

items.value: The book is anonymous, but the tradition attaching it to Mark is early and specific. Papias, writing around AD 130 and quoting an older source he calls "the elder," says that Mark became Peter's interpreter and wrote down accurately what he remembered of what Yahshua said and did, though not in order. That last phrase is an odd thing to invent as praise, which is part of why it is taken seriously.

The internal evidence fits. Peter is the first disciple named and the last, and the account is unusually unflattering to him - which is easier to explain if it came from him than if it did not. Several scenes carry the sort of detail an eyewitness keeps and a summariser drops: the cushion in the stern of the boat, the green grass, the number of the fish, the crowd sitting down in groups.

The audience is Roman and largely Gentile. Mark translates every Aramaic phrase he uses - Talitha cumi, Ephphatha, Abba, Eloi Eloi - and stops to explain Jewish handwashing custom in chapter 7, which Matthew never does because his readers already know. He uses Latin loanwords for Greek ones where a Roman would, and he measures time in Roman watches. In chapter 15 he names Simon of Cyrene as "the father of Alexander and Rufus," which only helps if the readers know who Alexander and Rufus are.
Mark is built in two halves with a hinge in the middle, and the hinge is a question.

For eight chapters the question is *who is this?* - asked by disciples in a boat, by scribes in a synagogue, by demons who already know. Then at Caesarea Philippi Yahshua asks it Himself, Peter answers "you are the Christ," and the Gospel turns. From that verse on the subject is not who He is but what He came to do, and the road runs one direction: toward Jerusalem and a cross. He predicts His death three times in three chapters, and each time the disciples respond by misunderstanding something about greatness.

There is also a frame around the whole thing. The first verse calls Him the Son of God. Nobody human says that again until chapter 15, when a Roman centurion watches Him die and says it. In between, only God and demons use the title. That is the argument of the book in its structure: the confession the reader is given at the start is the one a Gentile soldier arrives at by watching a crucifixion.
The word euthys - immediately, at once, straight away - appears in Mark about forty times, more than in the rest of the New Testament put together. Chapter 1 alone uses it eleven times.

It is easy to read that as breathlessness, and partly it is. But it also does something to the portrait. This is a Messiah who is always already on the way somewhere, who does not linger over His own miracles, and who repeatedly leaves a town at the exact moment it starts going well. The pace is the point, and it is worth not smoothing out when you read aloud.

Again and again in this Gospel, Yahshua silences people. He silences demons who name Him correctly. He tells the healed to say nothing. He warns the disciples not to repeat Peter's confession. Then in chapter 14, standing before the high priest with nothing left to lose, He answers the question plainly for the first time.

Scholars have argued for over a century about why. The reading this book takes is the plainest one: the title Messiah carried a set of expectations - a king, an army, Rome thrown out - and every one of them would have to be corrected before it could be safely accepted. He would not let people say who He was until they could be shown what that meant, and what it meant was a cross. Once the cross is in view, the silence ends.

Most place Mark in the 60s of the first century, around the persecution under Nero and the deaths of Peter and Paul - which would explain a Gospel written down at the moment the eyewitnesses started dying, and one that dwells at length on suffering, betrayal, and standing firm under trial.
Some argue for just after AD 70 on the strength of chapter 13. Readers who take predictive prophecy seriously will not find that decisive, and this book does not try to settle it.
Read Mark straight through at least once, in one sitting, before any of the apparatus. It takes well under two hours and the shape only shows at speed.
After that, take a chapter at a time. Read the introduction first, then the chapter itself, and come back to the notes and tables afterward; they will mean more once the text is in you.
If you are reading with others, the introductions are written to be read aloud. That is what they were for originally, and they still work best that way.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 1 - Immediately: A Gospel That Starts at a Run
chapters.title: Immediately: A Gospel That Starts at a Run
keyNotes: There is no genealogy and no birth narrative. Mark begins where the public ministry begins, which tells you what kind of book this is going to be (Mark 1:1).
"The beginning of the Good News" - arche - is the same word that opens Genesis in the Greek Old Testament. Something is starting (Mark 1:1).
"Son of God" in verse 1 is the frame of the whole Gospel. No human being says it again until a Roman centurion at the cross (Mark 1:1, 15:39).

Verse 2 is Mark's only formula quotation - and it is a composite. "Behold, I send my messenger" is Malachi 3:1 crossed with Exodus 23:20; "the voice of one crying" is Isaiah 40:3. He credits it to Isaiah, naming the major prophet for the blend, which was ordinary practice (Mark 1:2-3).
John's clothing is a costume with a meaning. Camel's hair and a leather belt is how 2 Kings describes Elijah, and Malachi had promised Elijah before the Day (Mark 1:6).
"The heavens parting" is schizo - torn, ripped. Mark uses that violent verb twice: here, and for the temple curtain at the moment He dies (Mark 1:10, 15:38).
The voice combines Psalm 2:7, spoken over the king, with Isaiah 42:1, spoken over the suffering servant. Both identities, in one sentence, before He has done anything (Mark 1:11).
"The Spirit drove him out" is ekballo - the same verb Mark uses for casting out demons. The Spirit does not suggest the wilderness (Mark 1:12).
Mark gives the temptation two verses where Matthew and Luke give it eleven, and adds a detail neither has: He was with the wild animals (Mark 1:13).
"The time is fulfilled" uses kairos, the appointed moment, not chronos, ordinary passing time (Mark 1:15).
The four fishermen leave immediately, and Mark does not tell us they had met Him before. John's Gospel says they had. Mark wants the abruptness (Mark 1:16-20).
Zebedee is left in the boat with hired servants - a detail that quietly says this was a business, not subsistence (Mark 1:20).
The astonishment in the synagogue is about authority, not content. A scribe cited other scribes; He cited nobody (Mark 1:22).
The demon gets His identity exactly right - the Holy One of God - and is silenced for it. Correct theology from the wrong mouth is still a problem (Mark 1:24-25).
"Be quiet" is phimoo, literally be muzzled - the word used for an ox (Mark 1:25).
Simon's mother-in-law "served them" - diakoneo, the word behind deacon, and the same verb used of the angels in verse 13 (Mark 1:13, 31).
The crowd waits until sunset to bring the sick, because the Sabbath had to end first (Mark 1:32).
At the height of the success in Capernaum He gets up before dawn, goes out alone to pray, and then leaves town. That pattern repeats all the way through (Mark 1:35-38).
"Moved with compassion" in verse 41 is disputed: a few early manuscripts read moved with anger. Either way He touches a man no one had touched in years (Mark 1:41).
The healed leper is told to say nothing, tells everyone, and the result is that Yahshua can no longer enter a town openly. The disobedience costs Him access (Mark 1:44-45).

intro: Open Matthew and there is a genealogy. Open Luke and there is Zechariah in the temple, and shepherds, and a census. Open John and there is the beginning of the world. Open Mark and there is one sentence, and then a man in a desert eating insects.

That is a decision, not an oversight. Mark writes for Romans - Gentiles, people who do not know the Hebrew Scriptures - and Romans wanted to know what a man did. So there is no childhood here, no waiting, no scene-setting. The beginning of the Good News, and the book is already moving.

But verse 1 contains the whole argument. Son of God. From here on no human being says that again. Demons do. God does, twice, out of the sky. But no person reaches it until chapter 15, when a Roman soldier who has just watched Him die says it out loud. Mark gives the answer on the first line and then makes the reader walk to the cross to hear a human arrive at it.

The quotation that follows is a composite, and its first half is the last thing the Old Testament had to say. Behold, I send my messenger is Malachi 3:1, crossed with Exodus 23:20; the voice crying in the wilderness is Isaiah 40:3. The silence that closed the prophets breaks at exactly the sentence it stopped on.

And John's clothing is a costume with a meaning. Camel's hair and a leather belt is how 2 Kings describes Elijah, and Malachi had promised Elijah before the Day. Anyone who knew those books knew what they were looking at.

At the baptism, one verb is worth the whole scene. The heavens parting translates schizo - torn, ripped open, violently. Mark uses that word exactly twice in the Gospel: here, and at the moment of death, when the temple curtain is torn from top to bottom. The book opens with heaven ripped and closes with the veil ripped, and the same verb ties them together.

The voice says two things at once. You are my Son is Psalm 2, spoken over the king. In whom I am well pleased is Isaiah 42, spoken over the servant who gets crushed. King and suffering servant, in one sentence, before He has healed anybody.
Then the wilderness, and Mark gives it two verses where Matthew gives eleven. But the verb is not gentle: the Spirit drove him out - the same word Mark uses for casting out demons.

After that the pace takes over. The word immediately appears eleven times in this chapter alone. Called, followed, taught, astonished; a demon shouting, a fever gone, a whole city at the door after sunset.

And in the middle of the busiest day recorded, verse 35: early in the morning, while it was still dark, He got up and went out alone to pray. When they find Him and report that everyone is looking for Him - which is what success sounds like - He says let us go somewhere else. He leaves the town that wants Him.

The chapter ends with a man who could not keep quiet. Told to say nothing, he tells everyone, and the result is a sentence worth sitting with: Jesus could no longer openly enter a city. Enthusiasm cost the ministry something real.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 2 - A Hole in the Roof, a Tax Booth, and the Lord of the Sabbath
chapters.title: A Hole in the Roof, a Tax Booth, and the Lord of the Sabbath
keyNotes: Chapter 2 begins a run of five confrontations in a row, escalating from muttering in the heart to a plot to kill (Mark 2:6, 16, 18, 24, 3:6).
A Capernaum roof was beams laid across walls, packed with branches and mud, reached by an outside stair. It could be dug through and repaired - which is why the friends could do it (Mark 2:4).
"Seeing their faith" - theirs, the four carrying him. The paralytic is not recorded as saying anything at all (Mark 2:5).
The scribes' premise is entirely correct: only God forgives sins. That is what makes the claim so large (Mark 2:7).
"Son of Man" appears here for the first time in Mark. It is His own preferred title, it comes from Daniel 7, and it is far less loaded than Messiah (Mark 2:10, Daniel 7:13).
Levi son of Alphaeus is the man Matthew's Gospel calls Matthew. Mark keeps the old name (Mark 2:14).
A tax booth on the Capernaum road collected duty on goods moving through - a Jew working for Rome against his neighbours, which is why the word sinner attaches (Mark 2:14).
Eating together was not casual. Reclining at a man's table declared that you accepted him (Mark 2:15).
"I came not to call the righteous" is not a statement that some people do not need calling. It is aimed at people who believe they do not (Mark 2:17).
The bridegroom image is a claim. In the prophets the bridegroom of Israel is Yahweh (Mark 2:19, Hosea 2:19-20).
"The days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away" is the first hint of the cross in Mark, dropped into an argument about fasting (Mark 2:20).

Unshrunk cloth on an old garment tears worse when it shrinks. New wine still fermenting bursts a skin that has already stretched once. Both images say the same thing: this will not be a patch on the existing arrangement (Mark 2:21-22).
Plucking grain by hand as you pass through a neighbour's field was explicitly permitted (Mark 2:23, Deuteronomy 23:25).
So the objection is not theft. It is the day - the rabbis counted plucking as reaping (Mark 2:24).

"At the time of Abiathar the high priest" is a genuine difficulty: 1 Samuel 21 names his father Ahimelech. The phrase may mean in the passage about Abiathar, who is the far better known of the two. This book does not pretend the problem is not there (Mark 2:26).
"The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath" appears only in Mark. Matthew and Luke both record the incident and neither has this line (Mark 2:27).
It is a statement about what the Sabbath is for, not about whether it stands. Made for man makes it a gift, and the argument is with those who had made it a burden (Mark 2:27).
"Lord even of the Sabbath" is a claim over something God made and God commanded (Mark 2:28).

further.desc: exposition of the roof, the forgiveness claim, and the scribes' objection

intro: Five confrontations begin here, and they escalate. First the scribes only think it. Then they say it to the disciples. Then they ask directly. Then they accuse. And by verse 6 of chapter 3 they are planning a killing.

A practical detail makes the opening scene work. A house in Capernaum had a flat roof - beams across the walls, branches and packed mud on top, and an outside staircase. Four men carrying a stretcher could get up there, and the roof could be dug through and patched afterwards. Which is what they did.
Then verse 5: seeing their faith. Theirs - the four. The man on the mat says nothing in this story from beginning to end. Somebody else's faith carried him into the room.

And notice what is said first. Not stand up, but your sins are forgiven - which is not what anyone had come for, and it starts the fight. The scribes are entirely right that only God forgives sins. That is not their error. They have understood the claim perfectly and drawn one of the only two possible conclusions.

Then Levi, sitting in a tax booth on the Capernaum road, taking money from his own neighbours for Rome. Follow me, and he goes - and then holds a dinner. The scandal is not the food but the table: in that world, reclining at a man's table said I accept you.

The question about fasting is answered with a wedding, which is a larger claim than it sounds, because in the prophets the bridegroom of Israel is Yahweh. And then, dropped almost casually into an argument about religious practice, comes the first shadow in the book: the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away.

The patch and the wineskins make the same point twice. What He brings is not a repair to the existing arrangement. Sew new cloth onto an old coat and the first wash tears a bigger hole than there was before.

The grain fields need care, because the passage gets misused. Plucking heads of grain while walking through a field was explicitly permitted by Deuteronomy 23. Nobody is accused of theft. The objection is the day, because the rabbis classified plucking as a form of reaping.

So the answer is not that the Sabbath does not matter. The answer is about what it is for - and the sentence that carries it appears only in Mark. Matthew and Luke both tell this story and neither records the line: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.

Made for man makes it a gift. What happens to a gift when thirty-nine categories of prohibited labour are built around it is that the people it was given to end up serving it. That is the argument. Not that the day is cancelled, but that it has been turned upside down.
And the last line is the largest claim yet: the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath. Lord of a day God made, blessed and commanded.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 3 - A Withered Hand, an Unforgivable Sin, and a Family Redefined
chapters.title: A Withered Hand, an Unforgivable Sin, and a Family Redefined
keyNotes: "They watched him" is paratereo - to watch closely, out of the corner of the eye, with intent. They came to the synagogue hoping for a healing they could prosecute (Mark 3:2).
The man is told to stand up in the middle of the room first. The healing is made deliberately public (Mark 3:3).
His question reframes the whole dispute: is it lawful to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill? Nobody answers, and by verse 6 they are doing the second one - on the Sabbath (Mark 3:4, 6).
Only Mark records the anger. "Looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts" - both at once, and the grief is what the anger is made of (Mark 3:5).
Pharisees and Herodians conspiring together is an unnatural alliance: one group despised Roman power, the other depended on it (Mark 3:6).
This is the earliest death plot in any of the Gospels - chapter 3 of 16 (Mark 3:6).
The crowd's geography is worth reading slowly: Idumaea, beyond the Jordan, Tyre and Sidon. That is Gentile territory, in a Gospel written for Gentiles (Mark 3:8).
The demons get the title right again, and again are silenced. Mark keeps making the same point (Mark 3:11-12).
"He appointed twelve, that they might be with him" - the being comes before the sending, and it is listed first (Mark 3:14).
Twelve is not a random number for a Jewish writer. It is the tribes, being reconstituted (Mark 3:14, Exodus 24:4).
Boanerges, Sons of Thunder, is one of the Aramaic phrases Mark stops to translate for readers who would not know it (Mark 3:17).
Every list of the twelve puts Peter first and Judas last, and each names Judas by what he did (Mark 3:16-19).
"His friends" in verse 21 translates a phrase that means those belonging to him - his family. Verse 31 confirms it: His mother and brothers arrive (Mark 3:21, 31).
"He is insane" is only in Mark. Matthew and Luke both omit it (Mark 3:21).
Beelzebul was a Philistine deity name repurposed as a title for Satan (Mark 3:22).
The strong man image assumes the house is being robbed. He is not negotiating with the strong man; He is tying him up (Mark 3:27).
The unforgivable sin has a stated context: they said He has an unclean spirit. Verse 30 exists to tell you what the sin was (Mark 3:29-30).

It is not a moment of anger or doubt. It is settled, deliberate insistence that the work of the Holy Spirit is demonic - and anyone frightened they have committed it is demonstrating a sensitivity that the sin itself has extinguished (Mark 3:29-30).
The family stands outside and sends for Him; the new family is sitting around Him (Mark 3:31-34).
"Whoever does the will of God" is the qualification - not belief only, and not blood (Mark 3:35).

intro: The argument that began in chapter 2 comes to a head in six verses.

A man with a withered hand, in a synagogue, on the Sabbath - and a crowd who watched him. The word means watching out of the corner of the eye, with intent. They are not hoping the man is healed. They are hoping the healing happens, so that they have something to use.

It is not done quietly. The man is told to stand up in the middle, where everyone can see, and then a question reframes the whole dispute: is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill?

Nobody answers. And then verse 6, where the irony becomes unbearable. They leave that synagogue and immediately begin planning how to kill Him - on the Sabbath. The question was whether the day was for saving or killing; they refused to answer it aloud and then answered it with their feet.

Verse 5 gives what no other Gospel does. He looked around at them with anger. Matthew has this story. Luke has this story. Neither mentions the anger. Only Mark records His face - and then names what the anger was made of: grief at the hardness of their hearts. The two are not opposites here.
Then the crowds, and the place names repay slow reading. Idumaea. Beyond the Jordan. Tyre and Sidon. That is Gentile country, and in a Gospel written for Gentiles the list is doing work.
Twelve are appointed, and the order of the reasons matters. That they might be with him comes first; that he might send them out comes second. Being before doing.

Then two accusations arrive from opposite directions, and Mark stacks them deliberately. His family come to take Him home because people are saying He is out of His mind - which only Mark records. Then scribes come down from Jerusalem with something far worse: he has Beelzebul.

The reply takes the accusation apart with plain logic. A kingdom divided cannot stand. Satan does not undermine himself. And then the strong man: nobody walks into a strong man's house and carries off his property without first tying him up. That is the claim - not negotiation with the strong man, but binding him.
Then the hardest words in the Gospel, and they need handling carefully, because they frighten people. Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness.

Verse 30 exists for exactly this reason: because they said, he has an unclean spirit. That is the sin. Not doubt. Not a bad thought. Not anger. It is looking straight at the work of the Spirit of God, knowing what it is, and calling it demonic - deliberately and settledly.

And the pastoral point follows from that. Anyone afraid of having committed this is demonstrating a sensitivity the sin itself has extinguished. The person described here is not lying awake worrying about it.

The chapter then ends gently. His family stand outside sending messages in, and He looks around at the people sitting on the floor of a crowded house and says: here. These are my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of God. It is not a rejection of His mother - she is in the room at Pentecost later. It is an enlargement, and the way in is doing the will of God.

chapters.title: Four Kinds of Ground, and a Man Asleep in a Sinking Boat
keyNotes: This is the first block of sustained teaching in Mark. Three chapters of action come first, and the parables arrive to explain why the action gets the reception it does (Mark 4:1-2).
In that country sowing came before ploughing, so scattering seed across a path or thorny ground was normal practice, not carelessness (Mark 4:3-7).
"Listen!" and "whoever has ears to hear" bracket the parable. The subject of the story is how you are hearing it (Mark 4:3, 9).
Thirty, sixty and a hundredfold is an extraordinary yield. Ordinary return in that soil was something like sevenfold or tenfold (Mark 4:8).
"The mystery of God's Kingdom" - mysterion is not a puzzle but something previously hidden and now disclosed (Mark 4:11).
Verse 12 quotes Isaiah 6:9-10, spoken when Isaiah was commissioned to a people who would not listen. The parables sort hearers rather than merely illustrate (Mark 4:12).
"Lest perhaps they should turn again and be forgiven" is the hardest line in the chapter. Matthew softens it to because; Mark keeps the sharper form (Mark 4:12).
"Don't you understand this parable? How will you understand all of the parables?" - the sower is the key that opens the rest (Mark 4:13).
The four soils are four ways of hearing, not four types of person. Three of them involve real reception and only one survives (Mark 4:15-20).
The rocky ground is not shallow enthusiasm at the start - it springs up faster than anything else. Speed is not the same as depth (Mark 4:5, 16-17).
The thorns are named precisely: cares, the deceitfulness of riches, and the desires for other things. Nothing on that list is a sin in itself (Mark 4:19).
The lamp saying assumes the answer. Nobody lights a lamp in order to hide it - which is why the secrecy of this Gospel is temporary (Mark 4:21-22).
"Take heed what you hear" and "with the measure you use" make hearing an act with consequences, not a passive event (Mark 4:24).
The seed growing secretly appears only in Mark. The farmer sleeps, the seed grows, and he does not know how (Mark 4:26-29).
"He puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come" quotes Joel 3:13, which is a harvest of judgment (Mark 4:29).
The mustard seed was proverbially the smallest thing a Jewish farmer handled - the point is the proverb, not botany (Mark 4:31).
Birds lodging in the branches echoes Daniel and Ezekiel, where a great tree sheltering birds is an empire (Mark 4:32).
"He himself was in the stern, asleep on the cushion" - the kind of detail an eyewitness keeps (Mark 4:38).
"Don't you care that we are dying?" is an accusation, not a request. Mark leaves it in (Mark 4:38).
He rebukes the wind and speaks to the sea using the same verb he used to muzzle the demon in chapter 1 (Mark 1:25, 4:39).
In the Hebrew Scriptures only Yahweh stills the sea. The disciples' question at the end is the right one (Mark 4:41, Psalm 107:29).
They are more frightened after the calm than during the storm (Mark 4:40-41).

intro: Three chapters of nonstop movement stop here for a chapter of teaching, and that is not a change of subject. Chapter 3 ended with His family calling Him mad and the scribes calling Him demonic. Chapter 4 explains why people hear the same words and end up in completely different places.

A farming detail rescues the parable from sounding like incompetence. In that country they sowed first and ploughed afterwards. A man scattering seed across a footpath, over rocky patches and into last year's thorns is not careless. That is simply how it was done. The seed goes everywhere.

Four grounds - and three of the four receive it. The path does not, but the rocky ground receives it with joy, and the thorny ground receives it and grows it. Two of the four have a real beginning and no ending.

The rocky ground repays attention, because it comes up fastest. Verse 5 says immediately it sprang up. It outgrew the good soil at the start. Speed is not depth, and what comes up overnight has usually not gone down.

And the thorns are named precisely: the cares of this age, the deceitfulness of riches, the desire for other things. Not one of them is a sin. That is what makes them dangerous - nobody repents of a full schedule.

Verses 11 and 12 are hard and should not be dodged. To you is given the mystery; to those outside, everything comes in parables, so that seeing they may see and not perceive. That is Isaiah 6, the words given to Isaiah when he was sent to people who had already decided not to listen. Parables are not simply illustrations. They sort hearers. Getting inside requires asking - which is exactly what the twelve do in verse 10.

The lamp settles something about the whole Gospel. Nobody lights a lamp in order to put it under a bucket. All the silencing in Mark - the demons, the healed leper, the disciples - is temporary. It is a lamp being carried to its stand, not a lamp being hidden.

Then a parable only Mark records, and it is a relief. A man scatters seed and goes to bed, and it grows, and he does not know how. The Kingdom does not wait on our understanding of the mechanism. Sometimes the most faithful thing available is sleep.

The mustard seed was proverbially the smallest thing a farmer handled, becoming the largest plant in the garden, with birds nesting in its shade - and that image is borrowed. In Daniel and Ezekiel, a great tree with birds in its branches is an empire.
Then evening comes and everything changes. A squall drops off the hills onto that lake fast, and the boat is filling.
And He is asleep. In the stern. On the cushion. Mark records where He was and what His head was on, which is the kind of thing only someone who was there remembers.
What they say is not a prayer. Teacher, do you not care that we are dying? That is an accusation, and Mark writes it down and leaves it there.

He rebukes the wind with the same verb used to muzzle the demon in chapter 1, and there is a great calm. And then the strangest line in the chapter: they were greatly afraid. More afraid after than during - because a storm is only a storm, and whatever is in the boat with them is something else.
Which produces the question the whole first half of this Gospel is asking. Who then is this? In the Hebrew Scriptures there is exactly one person who tells the sea what to do.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 5 - Legion, a Hem Touched in a Crowd, and a Little Girl Told to Get Up
chapters.title: Legion, a Hem Touched in a Crowd, and a Little Girl Told to Get Up
keyNotes: Three impossible cases in a row: a man no one can restrain, a condition twelve years old, and a death. Mark stacks them deliberately (Mark 5:2, 25, 35).
The far side of the lake is Gentile country - tombs, pigs, and Decapolis. Everything in this scene is unclean to a Jewish reader (Mark 5:1-2, 11, 20).
The man lives among tombs, cries out night and day, and cuts himself with stones. Mark spends four verses on the misery before anything happens (Mark 5:3-5).
He runs toward Yahshua and bows, then screams at Him not to torment him. Both at once (Mark 5:6-7).
"Son of the Most High God" is a title a Gentile would use. Even the demons speak in the local idiom (Mark 5:7).
A legion was a Roman formation of up to six thousand men. The name says occupation (Mark 5:9).
Two thousand pigs. In Gentile territory this is livestock, not contraband - and it is somebody's livelihood going over the cliff (Mark 5:11-13).
"Sitting, clothed, and in his right mind" is the whole healing in six words (Mark 5:15).
They are afraid of the healing, not of the demons they had lived beside for years, and they ask Him to leave. He goes (Mark 5:15-17).
The one man who begs to come with Him is refused, and told to go home and tell his own people. The silencing rule is reversed the moment the ground is Gentile (Mark 5:18-20).
Mark tells this story inside another one - the woman interrupts Jairus. He does that repeatedly, and the two halves always interpret each other (Mark 5:21-43).
A synagogue ruler falling at His feet in public is a costly act, given what chapter 3 said about synagogue authorities (Mark 5:22).
The woman's condition made her ritually unclean, and everything she touched with her (Mark 5:25, Leviticus 15:25-27).
"Had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse" - Luke the physician omits that line (Mark 5:26).
Twelve years bleeding; twelve years old. Mark gives both numbers, and they are not a coincidence in his telling (Mark 5:25, 42).
She reaches for His clothes, not His hand. The fringe of a garment is what a desperate person could reach without being seen (Mark 5:27-28).
He stops a crowd, in the middle of an emergency, to find one woman - and gives her time to tell the whole truth in public (Mark 5:30-33).
"Daughter" is the only time in the Gospels He calls a woman that. She is not sent away healed; she is sent away named (Mark 5:34).
The delay costs the girl her life, humanly speaking. That is part of the story's design (Mark 5:35).
"Don't be afraid, only believe" is said to a man who has just been told it is too late (Mark 5:36).
Professional mourners were hired quickly and loudly; the shift from wailing to ridicule in one verse tells you how genuine it was (Mark 5:38-40).
"Talitha cumi" is Aramaic, and Mark translates it - as he does every Aramaic phrase, for readers who do not know it. It is gentle: little girl, get up (Mark 5:41).
The last instruction is that somebody should give her something to eat (Mark 5:43).

intro: Three cases in a row, and each is further past hope than the last. A man nobody can restrain. A woman twelve years into an incurable condition. And then a death.
They land on the far shore, and everything about the location would unsettle a Jewish reader. Tombs. Pigs. Decapolis. It is Gentile ground, and unclean from the moment the boat touches it.

Mark spends four verses describing the man before anything happens. Living in the tombs. Chains torn apart. Nobody strong enough to subdue him. Night and day, screaming, cutting himself with stones. It is a portrait of someone entirely recognisable - a person everyone has given up on, living among the dead, hurting himself, and too strong to be helped.

Then the name. My name is Legion, for we are many. A legion was a Roman army unit of up to six thousand men, and in occupied territory that is not a neutral word. What is inside him is an occupying force.

The town's reaction is the most disturbing part of the chapter. They come out, see the man sitting, clothed and in his right mind - and they are afraid, and ask Jesus to leave. They had tolerated a screaming man in the tombs for years. One healing and a financial loss, and they want Him gone. And He goes, without argument.

And the one man who asks to come with Him is the only person refused. Go home. Tell your own people. Everywhere else in this Gospel the instruction is silence; here, on Gentile ground, it is go and tell.
Back across the water, Mark does what he does often: he begins one story, interrupts it with another, and finishes the first. The interruption is the point.

Jairus is a synagogue ruler - and synagogue authorities have not come off well in this book so far. He is on his knees in public in front of the man his colleagues are working to destroy. That costs him everything.

Then the interruption. A woman, twelve years bleeding, which under the law meant permanently unclean, and so was anything and anyone she touched. Twelve years of nobody being able to touch her. And Mark adds a line that Luke, a physician, quietly omits: she had suffered much under many physicians, spent everything she had, and was worse rather than better.
So she does not ask. She comes up behind Him in a crowd and reaches for the edge of His coat, because that is what people do when they are not allowed to be there.

And He stops. In the middle of an emergency, with a dying child at the other end of the street, He halts a crowd to find one woman - and she comes trembling and tells Him the whole truth, in public, all of it. He would not let her leave with only the healing. He made room for her to be known.
And He calls her daughter, which is the only time in the four Gospels He calls a woman that.

While He is doing it, the messengers arrive. Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the teacher any further. The delay cost the girl her life, and Mark means that to be felt, because the answer to it is: do not be afraid, only believe.
Twelve years bleeding. A girl twelve years old. Mark gives both numbers. One woman had been dying for exactly as long as the other had been alive.
Then a room cleared of professional mourners who went from wailing to laughing in a single verse. And two words of Aramaic, kept and translated: Talitha cumi. Little girl, get up.
And the last instruction is that somebody should get her something to eat. The dead are raised, and He is thinking about her breakfast.

chapters.title: No Honor at Home, a Head on a Platter, and Bread in a Deserted Place
keyNotes: Nazareth was a village of a few hundred people. Everyone in that synagogue had known Him since He was a child (Mark 6:1-3).
The offence is not the teaching - they concede the wisdom and the mighty works. The offence is that they know where He is from (Mark 6:2-3).
"The carpenter" is tekton, a builder in wood and stone. Only Mark gives Him the trade; Matthew calls Him the carpenter's son (Mark 6:3).
"The son of Mary" rather than the son of Joseph is unusual enough in that culture to be pointed (Mark 6:3).
Four brothers are named and sisters mentioned. Two of those brothers, James and Judah, later write letters in the New Testament (Mark 6:3).
"He could do no mighty work there" is a startling sentence, and Mark does not soften it (Mark 6:5).
He marvels twice in this Gospel: at the faith of a centurion elsewhere, and here at unbelief at home (Mark 6:6).
Two by two follows the requirement of two witnesses in the law (Mark 6:7, Deuteronomy 19:15).
The travel instructions are severe and specific: a staff and sandals, but no bread, no bag, no money. Dependence is the training (Mark 6:8-9).
Shaking dust off the feet was what a Jew did on leaving Gentile territory. Aimed at a Jewish town it is a hard sign (Mark 6:11).
"Anointed many with oil who were sick" is the only place in the Gospels the twelve do this (Mark 6:13, James 5:14).
The account of John's death is the longest passage in Mark not about Yahshua, and it sits between the sending of the twelve and their return - a flashback filling the gap (Mark 6:14-29).
Herod Antipas was a tetrarch, not a king; Mark uses the popular title (Mark 6:14).
"Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe... and he heard him gladly" is one of the saddest sentences in the Gospel. He liked listening to him (Mark 6:20).
The oath is the trap. He kills a man he admired rather than lose face in front of guests (Mark 6:26).
John's disciples come and take the body and lay it in a tomb - the same words used of Yahshua later (Mark 6:29).
"Come apart into a deserted place and rest awhile" is an instruction that immediately gets cancelled by a crowd (Mark 6:31-33).
"Like sheep without a shepherd" is a quotation. Moses used it praying for a successor (Mark 6:34, Numbers 27:17).
Two hundred denarii is roughly two-thirds of a labourer's annual wage - the disciples are pricing the impossible (Mark 6:37).
"Green grass" dates it to spring, near Passover, and is another eyewitness detail (Mark 6:39).
Sitting in ranks by hundreds and fifties is how Israel was organised in the wilderness (Mark 6:40, Exodus 18:21).
Twelve baskets - one each. Everyone who said it could not be done carried the evidence home (Mark 6:43).
The fourth watch is between three and six in the morning. They had been rowing most of the night (Mark 6:48).
"He would have passed by them" is strange until you notice that passing by is what God does to Moses and Elijah on the mountain (Mark 6:48, Exodus 33:22, 1 Kings 19:11).
"It is I" is ego eimi - I AM. It is the ordinary way to say it's me, and it is also the name (Mark 6:50).
"They hadn't understood about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened" applies to the disciples the same word used of the Pharisees in chapter 3 (Mark 3:5, 6:52).

intro: He goes home to a village of a few hundred people, every one of whom had watched Him grow up.

And they concede everything. Where did this man get these things? What is this wisdom? These mighty works? All of it granted. And then: is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, and the brother of James, Joses, Judah and Simon? Are his sisters not here with us?

That is the offence. Not that He is wrong - that He is theirs. They know the family. They know what He charged for a roof beam. Familiarity did not produce contempt exactly; it produced an inability to reconsider.

Then verse 5, one of the most sobering sentences in the Gospels. He could do no mighty work there. Mark could have written would not. He wrote could not. And verse 6 says He marvelled at their unbelief - one of only two occasions He is described as astonished, the other being a Roman soldier's faith.
So the twelve are sent out instead, two by two, with a severe packing list. A staff. Sandals. No bread, no bag, no money. It is not a test but a training; dependence cannot be learned in theory.

Then Mark does something unusual. Between the sending and the return he tells how John the Baptist died - the longest passage in this Gospel that is not about Yahshua. Its placement is the point. This is what happens to messengers.

And it is a story about a weak man. Verse 20 is one of the saddest verses in the Bible: Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and kept him safe; and when he heard him, he did many things, and he heard him gladly. He liked listening to him. He protected him. He knew exactly what John was.

Then a party, a dance, and a rash oath made in front of important people. And Herod is exceedingly sorry - and does it anyway. Because of his oaths, and because of his dinner guests. He killed a prophet he admired rather than look foolish in front of the chief men of Galilee.
The twelve return full of what they have done, and are told to come away and rest - and cannot, because the crowd runs around the lake on foot and arrives first.

And the response is not irritation. He had compassion, because they were like sheep without a shepherd - which is a quotation. Moses prayed exactly that when asking God to appoint a successor, so that the congregation would not be like sheep with no shepherd.

Then the arithmetic. The disciples price the impossible: two hundred denarii, most of a year's wages. And the question that reframes it is not what do you lack, but how many loaves do you have? Go and see.

The details Mark keeps are worth noticing. Green grass, so it is spring. Groups of hundreds and fifties, which is how Israel was organised in the wilderness. And twelve baskets left over - one each. Every man who said it could not be done carried the evidence home.

Then the strangest verse in the chapter. He is walking on the water in the fourth watch - between three and six in the morning - and Mark says He meant to pass by them. That reads as cruelty until you notice where the phrase comes from. Yahweh passed by Moses in the cleft of the rock. Yahweh passed by Elijah at the mouth of the cave. Passing by is what God does when He shows Himself.
And what He says is ego eimi. It is I - the ordinary way to say it is me, and also the name given at the burning bush.

The chapter ends on a line about the disciples that should stop any reader: they had not understood about the loaves, and their hearts were hardened. That is the same word Mark used of the Pharisees in chapter 3. It is possible to be in the boat, to have carried a basket, and still not see.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 7 - Corban, Crumbs Under the Table, and One Word: Be Opened
chapters.title: Corban, Crumbs Under the Table, and One Word: Be Opened
keyNotes: A delegation has come down from Jerusalem. This is not local opposition any more - the capital is taking an interest (Mark 7:1).
Verses 3 and 4 are Mark explaining Jewish custom to readers who do not know it. Matthew tells the same story and explains nothing, because his readers already understand (Mark 7:3-4).
The charge is not breaking the law of Moses. Handwashing before ordinary meals was a rabbinic tradition, required of priests in the temple and extended by custom to everyone else (Mark 7:5).
He answers with Isaiah 29:13 - lips near, heart far - and it is the only place the quotation and the accusation match this exactly (Mark 7:6-7).
"Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men" is the hinge of the argument. The problem is not that tradition exists; it is tradition given the authority of Scripture (Mark 7:7).
Then a specific case. Corban is a real word from the sacrificial system - an offering, something devoted. Mark translates it, as he does every Aramaic term (Mark 7:11).
The abuse was declaring assets Corban so they could not be used to support ageing parents - and the vow was treated as binding even when the money never reached the temple (Mark 7:11-12).
"Making void the word of God by your tradition" - and the commandment being voided is the fifth, honour your father and mother (Mark 7:10, 13).
"There is nothing outside a man that going in can defile him" is said in a dispute about unwashed hands, and the disciples themselves call it a parable (Mark 7:15, 17).
Verse 16 is not in the earliest manuscripts. The WEB prints it; most modern translations omit it or footnote it (Mark 7:16).

**Verse 19 needs care.** The Greek ends with a participle - katharizon panta ta bromata, cleansing all foods - and it can attach to two different words. The WEB attaches it to the digestive process: food goes to the stomach and out to the latrine, thus purifying all foods. Most modern versions attach it to the speaker and render it as an editorial comment: "(Thus he declared all foods clean.)" (Mark 7:19).
Both readings are defensible. The manuscripts differ on whether the participle is masculine or neuter, and that is what the argument turns on (Mark 7:19).
What is not in dispute is the subject under discussion: nobody in this scene is eating anything unclean. The question raised in verses 2 and 5 is unwashed hands (Mark 7:2, 5, 19).

It is also worth noticing that years later, on a rooftop in Joppa, Peter - who was standing here - says he has never eaten anything unholy. Whatever this verse settled, he did not understand it as settled that day (Mark 7:19, Acts 10:14).
The vice list that follows is the actual answer to what defiles, and every item on it is internal (Mark 7:21-22).
Tyre and Sidon is Gentile territory, and He goes there to be unrecognised and fails (Mark 7:24).
"A Greek, a Syrophoenician by race" - Mark labels her twice, so no reader can miss that she is an outsider (Mark 7:26).
"Let the children be filled first" contains the concession before the refusal. First implies a second (Mark 7:27).
The word for dogs is the diminutive - the little dogs, household animals under the table, not the scavengers of the street (Mark 7:27).
She does not dispute the picture; she extends it, and He answers the argument rather than the need: for this saying, go your way (Mark 7:28-29).
This is the only healing in Mark performed at a distance, and the only time anyone wins an exchange with Him (Mark 7:29-30).
The deaf man is taken away from the crowd first - a private healing for a man who could not hear the crowd anyway (Mark 7:33).
"He sighed" - the word is a groan. He is not performing (Mark 7:34).
Ephphatha is Aramaic, and Mark keeps the sound of it before translating (Mark 7:34).
"He has done all things well" echoes Genesis - God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good (Mark 7:37).
"He makes the deaf hear and the mute speak" is close to Isaiah 35, where those are the signs of God coming to save (Mark 7:37, Isaiah 35:5-6).

intro: The opposition has been local until now. Here a delegation arrives from Jerusalem, and the subject is handwashing.

It is worth being precise about what is and is not at issue, because this passage gets misused in both directions. Nobody is accused of breaking the law of Moses. Washing hands before an ordinary meal is not in the Torah - it was required of priests handling holy things, and the tradition of the elders had extended it to everybody, everywhere, always.

So the answer is not that the law does not matter. The answer is Isaiah: this people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. The problem is not that traditions exist. It is that a human rule has been given the authority of a divine one.

Then a specific example, and it is devastating. Corban was a real category - something dedicated to God. What some men were doing was declaring their assets Corban so that when their parents grew old and needed help, the money was technically unavailable. The vow was held binding, the parents went without, and the fifth commandment was cancelled by a religious technicality.
That is the charge: you make void the word of God by your tradition. Not by rebellion, but by piety.

Verse 19 needs slow handling, because translations differ and readers will notice. This text says the food goes into the stomach and out into the latrine, thus purifying all foods. Most modern versions instead carry a bracketed comment: thus he declared all foods clean.

Both come from a single Greek participle meaning cleansing, and the whole question is which word it attaches to. Attached to the latrine, the digestive process is what purges. Attached to the speaker back in verse 18, it is Mark adding an editorial note. The manuscripts themselves disagree on the ending of that participle, which is why translators divide.

The argument is not settled, and this book does not pretend otherwise. But two things are worth holding. First, the question on the table in verses 2 and 5 is unwashed hands, not what is on the plate; nobody in the scene is eating anything the law forbids. Second, Peter was standing here - and years later, on a rooftop in Joppa, shown a sheet full of animals and told to eat, he says he has never eaten anything unholy. Whatever this verse means, the man who heard it did not walk away thinking the question closed.
Then He leaves the country altogether, goes up to Tyre, and tries to be anonymous. And a Greek woman - Mark labels her twice as an outsider - asks for her daughter.
And He says the hardest thing He says to anyone in this Gospel. Let the children be filled first; it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs.

But two things are buried in it. First implies second: the children are fed first, which means somebody eats afterwards. And the word for dogs is not the street scavenger but the diminutive - the little dog under the table, part of the household.

She hears both. Yes, Lord - and even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs. She does not dispute the picture; she stands inside it and finishes it. And the reply is: for this saying, go your way. Not for your faith, not for your need. For this saying. She is the only person in the Gospels who wins an exchange with Him, and He seems delighted by it.

The chapter ends with a deaf man taken away from the crowd, in private, because a crowd is no use to a man who cannot hear it. Fingers in the ears. Spit on the tongue. A look at the sky, and a groan. And one word in His own language, kept before it is translated: Ephphatha. Be opened.
And the verdict of the onlookers is that he has done all things well, making the deaf hear and the mute speak - which is Isaiah 35, the list of signs for the day God Himself comes to save.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 8 - Trees Walking, and the Question the Whole Book Was Asking
chapters.title: Trees Walking, and the Question the Whole Book Was Asking
keyNotes: This chapter is the hinge of Mark. Everything before it asks who He is; everything after it moves toward the cross (Mark 8:29, 31).
The four thousand is a second feeding, not a duplicate of the first. The numbers, the location and the baskets all differ (Mark 6:44, 8:9).
This crowd has been with Him three days and includes people who came a long way - in Gentile territory, after the trip to Tyre and Decapolis (Mark 8:2-3).
The word for basket here is different from chapter 6: a large hamper rather than a small wicker lunch basket (Mark 8:8, 19-20).
Twelve baskets for Israel, seven for the nations, is how many readers have taken the two numbers - and He makes the disciples recite both (Mark 8:19-20).
The disciples ask where anyone could get bread in a deserted place, having watched Him do exactly that (Mark 8:4).
"He sighed deeply in his spirit" - Mark keeps recording what His face and breath were doing (Mark 8:12).
No sign will be given. In Matthew there is an exception for Jonah; in Mark the refusal is flat (Mark 8:12).
Yeast works invisibly and changes the whole lump - which is why it stands for an influence rather than a doctrine (Mark 8:15).
The yeast of Herod and the yeast of the Pharisees are opposite errors: political accommodation and religious rigidity (Mark 8:15).
They hear a warning about yeast and conclude He is annoyed about catering (Mark 8:16).
"Is your heart still hardened? Having eyes, don't you see?" applies to the twelve the language used of Israel's blindness in the prophets (Mark 8:17-18, Jeremiah 5:21).
The blind man of Bethsaida is the only healing in the Gospels that happens in two stages, and it is placed immediately before Peter's confession on purpose (Mark 8:22-26).
"I see men; for I see them like trees walking" is real sight and wrong sight at the same time - which is exactly Peter's position six verses later (Mark 8:24, 29-33).
Caesarea Philippi sat beneath a cliff full of pagan shrines and a temple to Caesar. He asks who He is in the most religiously crowded place available (Mark 8:27).
The public answers are all respectable and all inadequate: John, Elijah, one of the prophets (Mark 8:28).
"But who do you say that I am" is the question the first half of the book has been building to, and Peter gets it right (Mark 8:29).
"He commanded them to tell no one" comes immediately after the right answer - because the word Christ carried expectations that had to be corrected first (Mark 8:30).
"He began to teach them" marks a new phase. From here the passion is taught openly (Mark 8:31).
"Must suffer" - dei, it is necessary. Not an accident or a defeat (Mark 8:31).
Peter takes Him aside and rebukes Him - the same verb used for rebuking demons and storms (Mark 8:32).
"Get behind me, Satan" is said to the man who has just confessed correctly, and it echoes the wilderness: an offer of a crown without a cross (Mark 8:33).
"You have in mind the things of men" is the diagnosis, and it is not wickedness. It is ordinary human sense (Mark 8:33).
Take up your cross was not a metaphor to that audience. They had seen men carry crossbeams through Galilee (Mark 8:34).
"Life" in verses 35 to 37 is psuche - life, soul, self. The same word is doing all the work in each verse (Mark 8:35-37).

intro: If Mark has a spine, this is the vertebra it bends on.

Before the turn, a second feeding - and readers sometimes assume Mark has told one story twice. He has not. Different crowd, different numbers, different place, and a different word for basket. And crucially, this one happens on the Gentile side. Chapter 6 fed Israel; chapter 8 feeds the nations.
The disciples ask where anyone could find bread in a deserted place, having personally carried twelve baskets of leftovers home not long before.

Then the Pharisees want a sign from heaven, and Mark says He sighed deeply in his spirit - a groan. The refusal is flat: no sign will be given to this generation. A sign would not have fixed them. They had just watched thousands eat.

Then the boat, and one of the sadder comic exchanges in the Gospels. He warns them about the yeast of the Pharisees and the yeast of Herod - two opposite ways of going wrong, religious rigidity on one side and political convenience on the other - and they conclude He is annoyed about catering.

And the questions that follow are the hardest in the book. Do you not yet perceive? Is your heart still hardened? Having eyes, do you not see? Having ears, do you not hear? Do you not remember? That language comes straight out of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, where it described Israel's blindness. It is now aimed at the twelve.
And exactly there Mark places a healing found nowhere else in the Gospels: a blind man healed in two stages.

He spits, touches the man's eyes, and asks whether he sees anything. And the man says he sees people, but they look like trees walking. That is real sight - he was blind and now is not. It is also wrong sight. So a second touch follows.
Hold that picture, because the next scene is Peter.

Caesarea Philippi is worth locating. It sat beneath a cliff full of niches for pagan gods, near a temple built for Caesar. In the most religiously crowded place in the region, He asks who people say He is.
The answers are respectful and inadequate. John the Baptist. Elijah. One of the prophets. Every one a compliment, and every one too small.
But who do you say that I am? And Peter gets it right. You are the Christ.
And immediately they are told to say nothing, and He begins teaching that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. Must - it is necessary. This is not a plan going wrong.
And Peter takes Him aside and rebukes Him, using the verb Mark used for rebuking demons and rebuking the storm. This is not advice; it is correction.

And the answer is the sharpest sentence in the Gospel: get behind me, Satan - said to the man who six verses earlier gave the right answer. He saw who Jesus was and could not see what it meant. He is the man seeing trees walking.

The diagnosis is worth noticing. Not: you are wicked. You have in mind the things of men. Ordinary human sense - of course you protect the person you love from suffering. That is what made it satanic. It was the wilderness offer again: have the crown, skip the cross.
And then the crowd is called over, because what follows is for everybody. If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross.

That phrase has been made gentle and it was not gentle. Those people had watched condemned men carry a crossbeam through their own streets. To take up a cross was to walk out of your life as a dead man walking - asked on the same afternoon they finally worked out who He was.

keyNotes: "Some standing here will not taste death until they see God's Kingdom come with power" has been read of the transfiguration six days later, the resurrection, Pentecost, and the fall of Jerusalem. The placement immediately before verse 2 favours the first (Mark 9:1-2).
"After six days" is unusually precise for Mark, and matches Moses waiting six days before God called him into the cloud (Mark 9:2, Exodus 24:16).
"He was changed into another form" is metamorphoo - transfigured. The change is in Him, not in the light around Him (Mark 9:2).
Mark describes the whiteness by way of laundry, because he is Mark: whiter than any launderer on earth could get them (Mark 9:3).
"Elijah and Moses" - Mark puts Elijah first, which no other Gospel does (Mark 9:4).
Moses died and was buried by God; Elijah did not die at all. Both had met God on this kind of mountain (Mark 9:4).
Peter offers to build three shelters, which would put Moses and Elijah on a level with Him - and Mark tells us plainly he was talking because he was terrified (Mark 9:5-6).
The voice corrects the offer without addressing it: this is my beloved Son - listen to him. Not to the three of them (Mark 9:7).
The cloud is the shekinah of the wilderness, and the words repeat the baptism with one addition - listen to him (Mark 1:11, 9:7).
"They saw no one with them any more, except Jesus only" (Mark 9:8).
The silence order now has an expiry date for the first time: until the Son of Man has risen (Mark 9:9).
They discuss what rising from the dead could mean. They believed in a general resurrection; what they cannot place is one man rising in the middle of history (Mark 9:10).
The Elijah question comes straight from Malachi 4:5, and He answers that Elijah has come already and was treated as they wished (Mark 9:11-13).
The glory on the mountain and the chaos at its foot are placed side by side deliberately (Mark 9:2-8, 14-18).
The father's description - thrown down, foaming, grinding teeth, wasting away, thrown into fire and water since childhood - is the longest medical description in Mark (Mark 9:18, 21-22).
"If you can do anything" is met with "if you can" thrown back at him. The question is not Yahshua's ability (Mark 9:22-23).
"I believe. Help my unbelief" is one of the most honest sentences in Scripture, and it is answered (Mark 9:24).
The boy looks dead afterwards, and Yahshua takes him by the hand and raises him - the same words used of Jairus' daughter (Mark 5:41, 9:27).
"And fasting" in verse 29 is missing from the earliest manuscripts. The WEB prints it (Mark 9:29).
The second passion prediction is met with silence, because they were afraid to ask (Mark 9:31-32).
They argue about who is greatest on the same road where He has just said He will be killed (Mark 9:33-34).
"He sat down" - the posture of a teacher about to say something formal (Mark 9:35).
Children in that world had no status to borrow. Setting one in the middle is not sentimental (Mark 9:36-37).
John's complaint - he was not following us - gets answered with a wider circle than the twelve wanted (Mark 9:38-40).
A cup of water is the smallest possible kindness, and it is the one that will not lose its reward (Mark 9:41).
The millstone is the large one, turned by a donkey, not a hand mill (Mark 9:42).
Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where children had been burned to Molech and where refuse later smouldered. It is a real place used as an image (Mark 9:43).
Verses 44 and 46 repeat verse 48 and are absent from the earliest manuscripts. The WEB prints all three (Mark 9:44, 46, 48).
"Their worm does not die" is the last verse of Isaiah, and it describes corpses, not conscious torment (Mark 9:48, Isaiah 66:24).
Salt was added to every offering under the law, and it both preserves and stings (Mark 9:49, Leviticus 2:13).
"Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another" is the answer to the argument that started the section (Mark 9:34, 50).

intro: Six days after Peter got it right and got it wrong, three of them go up a mountain.
The word is metamorphoo - transfigured, changed in form. This is not light shining on Him. It is something coming out from inside that had been there all along and had been held back.
And Mark describes it as only Mark would: His clothes were whiter than any launderer on earth could get them. A housekeeping comparison for the glory of God.

Then Elijah and Moses - and Mark puts Elijah first, which no other Gospel does. Two men: one God buried Himself in a grave nobody has found, and one who never died. Both had met God on a mountain like this one.
Peter starts talking, and Mark - who had this from Peter - tells us exactly why: he did not know what to say, because they were terrified. Three shelters, one each. Three equal shelters.
The voice does not argue with the offer. It simply says: this is my beloved Son. Listen to him. Not to the three of them. And when they look up, Moses and Elijah are gone and there is Jesus only.

Then they come down the mountain straight into a mess - a crowd, scribes arguing, nine disciples who have failed publicly, and a father whose son has been convulsing since childhood. Thrown down, foaming, grinding his teeth, wasting away, thrown into fire and into water. That is a man who has spent years pulling his child out of fireplaces and off riverbanks.
And he says: if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us. If you can - and notice help us, not help him. The whole family carries this.
The phrase is turned back on him, because the doubt was never on the other side.

And then the father says the sentence worth writing over the door of any church. I believe. Help my unbelief. Both at once, out loud, in front of everyone, with tears. And it is enough. The boy is healed - not because the man got his faith tidy, but because he brought the mess of it to the right person.

They pass through Galilee quietly, and a second time He says He will be handed over and killed and rise. Mark says they did not understand, and were afraid to ask - which is its own kind of honesty. They had seen what happened the last time somebody questioned Him about this.
Then Capernaum, and a question about what they were arguing about on the road, and the guilty silence of people who know exactly what they were arguing about.
They were arguing about which of them was greatest. On the same walk where He had just told them He was going to be executed.
And there is no shouting. He sits down - the posture of a teacher about to say something formal - and says that anyone who wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.

Then a child is set in the middle of them, and the sentiment has to be stripped off. In that world a child had no status to lend anybody. Taking a child in your arms gained you nothing. That is precisely the point.

Then John, still policing the boundaries: we saw someone casting out demons who is not one of us, and we stopped him. And the answer widens the circle past where the twelve wanted it - whoever is not against us is for us.

Then the hard sayings. A millstone. A hand, a foot, an eye. And Gehenna, which is a real place - the valley just outside Jerusalem where children had once been burned to Molech and where the city's refuse smouldered afterwards. He is not inventing an image; He is pointing over the wall.

And the hyperbole does what hyperbole does. Nobody in the history of the church has read this as surgical instruction. What it says is that there is nothing you own, nothing you do and nothing you look at that is worth more than your life.

It ends with salt. Every offering was salted. Salt preserves, and salt stings, and salt on a wound is not gentle. Have salt in yourselves - and be at peace with one another, which brings the whole section back to twelve men arguing on a road about which of them mattered most.

keyNotes: The geography turns here. From this chapter on, everything is a journey toward Jerusalem (Mark 10:1, 32).
The divorce question is a trap in more ways than one: Herod Antipas had executed John over exactly this subject, and they are now in Herod's territory beyond the Jordan (Mark 10:1-2, 6:17-18).
"What did Moses command you?" - He asks for the command and they answer with a permission. The distinction is the whole argument (Mark 10:3-4).
"For your hardness of heart" locates the reason for the concession in the people, not in the provision (Mark 10:5).
He goes behind Deuteronomy to Genesis, and quotes two verses from creation rather than one from the law (Mark 10:6-8).
"What God has joined together" makes marriage something God did, not only something two people agreed (Mark 10:9).
Mark's version has no exception clause. Matthew records one - except for sexual immorality - and Mark does not. This book does not pretend that difference is not there (Mark 10:11, Matthew 19:9).
Verse 12 assumes a wife could initiate divorce, which Jewish law did not generally allow but Roman law did. Mark is writing for Romans (Mark 10:12).
"Moved with indignation" is a strong word, and this is the only place in the Gospels it is used of Him (Mark 10:14).
Receiving the Kingdom like a child is about receiving, not about innocence. A child in that world could only take what was given (Mark 10:15).
He does not merely permit the children; He picks them up and blesses them (Mark 10:16).
The man runs and kneels - undignified for someone of his standing - and asks what he must do to inherit. Inheritance is not usually something you earn (Mark 10:17).
"Why do you call me good" is not a denial of goodness. It is an invitation to follow the word to its conclusion (Mark 10:18).
The commandments listed are all from the second table, the ones about neighbours - with "do not defraud" standing in where you would expect "do not covet" (Mark 10:19).
That substitution may be the point: defrauding is coveting with a business plan (Mark 10:19).
"Jesus looking at him loved him" is only in Mark, and it changes the whole scene (Mark 10:21).
"Taking up the cross" at the end of verse 21 is absent from many manuscripts. The WEB prints it (Mark 10:21).
He goes away sorrowful and is allowed to go. Nobody runs after him (Mark 10:22).
The camel and the needle is deliberate hyperbole. The old story about a gate called the Needle's Eye has no evidence behind it before the middle ages (Mark 10:25).
The disciples' astonishment assumes wealth is a sign of God's favour - which is why they ask who then can be saved (Mark 10:26).
"With men it is impossible" is the answer, and it applies to everyone, not only the rich (Mark 10:27).
The hundredfold list in verse 30 repeats the list in verse 29 with one omission: there is no wife in the return. And it adds two words - with persecutions (Mark 10:29-30).
"Jesus was going in front of them, and they were amazed; and those who followed were afraid" - Mark shows us the body language of the whole group (Mark 10:32).
The third prediction is the most detailed: condemned, handed to Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed (Mark 10:33-34).
James and John ask for thrones immediately after that. Matthew has their mother ask; Mark lets them ask for themselves (Mark 10:35-37, Matthew 20:20).
The cup is an Old Testament image for a portion appointed by God, often of wrath (Mark 10:38).
The two places at His right and left are eventually occupied - by two criminals (Mark 10:37, 15:27).
"It shall not be so among you" reverses the ordinary shape of authority rather than adjusting it (Mark 10:43).
"A ransom for many" - lutron, the price paid to free a slave or a captive. It is the clearest statement of purpose in Mark (Mark 10:45).
Bartimaeus is named, which is unusual, and Mark translates the name for readers who do not know Aramaic: son of Timaeus (Mark 10:46).
"Son of David" is a messianic title, shouted publicly for the first time in this Gospel - and this time He does not silence it (Mark 10:47-48).
A beggar's cloak was his licence to beg and his only shelter. Throwing it off is not a detail about clothing (Mark 10:50).
He is asked the same question James and John were asked - what do you want me to do for you - and gives a completely different answer (Mark 10:36, 51).
"He followed Jesus on the way" - and the way leads to Jerusalem (Mark 10:52).

intro: From here the road runs one direction. Mark says twice in this chapter that they are going up to Jerusalem, and by verse 32 it has a mood attached to it.

It opens with a trap sharper than it looks. They are beyond the Jordan, which is Herod's territory - and Herod had beheaded John the Baptist for saying something about a marriage. Answering this question wrongly could mean not leaving the district.
The exchange in verses 3 and 4 is the whole argument. He asks what Moses commanded. They answer with what Moses allowed. A concession has been turned into a permission slip.

So He goes back behind Moses - not to Deuteronomy but to Genesis. Male and female, one flesh, from the beginning of creation. And then: what God has joined together, let no man separate. Which makes a marriage something God did.

One difference should be stated plainly. Mark's version carries no exception. Matthew records except for sexual immorality; Mark does not. Anyone who has been through a divorce deserves better than a flattening in either direction. What stands here is Mark, and Mark is absolute - and Mark is also the Gospel that has spent nine chapters showing a man who forgives.

Then the children, and one word worth stopping on: indignant. It is the only place in the Gospels that word is used of Him, and it is aimed at His own disciples for turning away people who could do nothing for Him.
Receiving the Kingdom like a child is not about innocence or simplicity. A child in that world owned nothing and could earn nothing. The only thing a child could do with a gift was take it.

Which sets up the next scene. A man comes running - grown men of standing did not run - kneels, and asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. The collision is inside his own sentence: nobody earns an inheritance.

The commandments listed are all the ones about how people treat each other. But one is missing. Do not covet is absent, and in its place stands do not defraud, which is not one of the ten. That looks deliberate, because defrauding is what coveting looks like once it has a business plan.
The man says he has kept them all since he was young. And then comes the line only Mark records, and it changes everything: Jesus, looking at him, loved him.
This is not a trap being sprung. It is love telling a man the truth about the one thing that owns him. Sell what you have. Give it away. Come and follow me.
And his face falls, and he goes away sorrowful, and nobody chases him. That is one of the hardest verses in the Gospel. He let him go.

Then the camel and the needle, and it should not be rescued. There was no gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye; that story appears roughly a thousand years too late. He meant a sewing needle and a camel, and He meant impossible - which is exactly what the disciples heard, since their reply is: then who can be saved? The answer is nobody, unaided. With men it is impossible.
Then the third prediction, the most detailed yet: condemned, handed to Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed.
And James and John come straight over and ask for the two best seats.

The badness of that has to be felt. He has just described His own execution, and the reply is a request for cabinet positions. The response is patient - you do not know what you are asking - and true in a way they will only understand later, because those two places at His right and left do get filled. By two thieves, on two crosses.

And then verse 45, the sentence the whole book has been walking toward. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many. Ransom is the price paid to buy a slave out.

Then Jericho, and a blind man who will not be quieted. Told to be silent he shouts louder, and what he shouts is Son of David - a royal, messianic title, out loud, in public. And for the first time in this Gospel nobody is told to keep it quiet.
And he throws off his cloak, which was a beggar's licence and his only blanket. He threw away the thing he had been sitting on for years to reach a man who had not healed him yet.

And he is asked the same question James and John were asked - what do you want me to do for you? Same words, completely different answer. And the man who could not see ends the chapter following Him down the road.
