chapters.title: A Borrowed Colt, a Barren Tree, and Tables on the Floor
keyNotes: Mark's account covers a Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, and he dates them carefully - the next day, in the morning, again to Jerusalem (Mark 11:12, 20, 27).
A colt on which no one has ever sat is what was required for a sacred purpose (Mark 11:2, Numbers 19:2).
The whole donkey scene is a deliberate enactment of Zechariah 9:9, which Mark expects his readers not to know - he never quotes it (Mark 11:7, Zechariah 9:9).
A king coming on a donkey rather than a horse is a claim about the kind of king He is (Mark 11:7).
Hosanna means save now - it is a prayer, not a cheer (Mark 11:9).
The crowd quotes Psalm 118, which pilgrims sang going up to the feast, and adds a line about the kingdom of David that is not in the psalm (Mark 11:9-10).
The entry ends with an anticlimax that only Mark records: He looks around at everything, and goes back out to Bethany because it is late (Mark 11:11).
The fig tree and the temple are one story, not two. Mark splits the tree in half and puts the temple inside it - the same technique as Jairus and the woman (Mark 11:12-21).
"For it was not the season for figs" looks unfair until you know that a fig tree in leaf should carry early fruit; leaves without fruit is a false advertisement (Mark 11:13).
A tree making a show of life with nothing to eat on it, immediately before a temple full of activity and empty of God, is the whole point (Mark 11:13-17).
The tables were where pilgrims changed Roman coins - which carried Caesar's image - into temple currency, and rates were set by the sellers (Mark 11:15).
This happened in the Court of the Gentiles, the only place a non-Jew could pray (Mark 11:15-17).
He quotes Isaiah 56 - a house of prayer for all the nations - and only Mark keeps the last three words (Mark 11:17, Isaiah 56:7).
"A den of robbers" is Jeremiah 7, spoken in the gate of the temple just before the first one was destroyed. The audience would have caught it (Mark 11:17, Jeremiah 7:11).
A den is not where thieves rob. It is where they feel safe afterwards (Mark 11:17).
The plot to kill Him is now the response of the chief priests, not just the Pharisees (Mark 11:18).
"Have faith in God" is said standing beside a dead tree that had promised fruit (Mark 11:22).
"This mountain" is spoken within sight of the temple mount, and possibly of the Mount of Olives, which Zechariah says will be split (Mark 11:23, Zechariah 14:4).
The prayer promise is immediately qualified by forgiveness - the two are joined (Mark 11:24-25).
Verse 26 is absent from the earliest manuscripts. The WEB prints it (Mark 11:26).
The question about authority is a legal challenge: who ordained you (Mark 11:28).
He answers a question with a question, which was a normal rabbinic move, not evasion (Mark 11:29-30).
Their reasoning is recorded, and it is entirely political - they calculate the answer rather than seek it (Mark 11:31-32).
"We don't know" is a lie, and He declines to give truth to people who will not tell it (Mark 11:33).

intro: Three days are covered here, and Mark dates them carefully. Sunday, the entry. Monday, the tree and the temple. Tuesday, the questions.
The entry is deliberate theatre. He sends for a colt that has never been ridden - the requirement for an animal used for something holy - and rides into Jerusalem on it.

Mark never quotes Zechariah here. He does not need to. Everyone lining that road knew it: rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes to you, humble, riding on a donkey. A conquering general came on a horse; a king coming in peace came on a donkey. The transport was the sermon.
And the crowd shouts Hosanna, which has been turned into a happy word and is not one. It means save now. It is a cry for help.

Then the strangest anticlimax in the Gospels, and only Mark records it. He rides in, the crowd is shouting, He goes to the temple - and looks around at everything. And then, because it is getting late, goes back out to Bethany for the night.
That verse is doing something. He inspected it, like a man walking round a building the day before the work starts.
Then the fig tree, which makes readers uncomfortable, because it looks petty and because Mark says plainly it was not the season for figs.

Here is what makes sense of it. A fig tree in that country produces small early fruit at the same time as its leaves, before the main crop. A tree in full leaf is advertising. Leaves and nothing underneath means the tree has made a promise it cannot keep.
And watch the arrangement. Mark starts the tree, interrupts himself with the temple, then returns to the tree. That is his sandwich technique, and it always means the two halves explain each other.
So He walks into a temple in full leaf. Noise, activity, commerce, sacrifice, crowds. And nothing to eat.
The tables were in the Court of the Gentiles - the only part of that building where a non-Jewish person could stand and pray - and it had become a currency exchange and a livestock market.
And He quotes two prophets. My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations - and Mark alone keeps that last phrase, which is exactly what the courtyard was for.
And then a den of robbers, which is Jeremiah 7 - said standing in the gate of the first temple, shortly before it was flattened. Anyone who knew the Scriptures heard the threat inside the quotation.

And notice what a den is. Not where a robber robs, but where he goes afterwards to feel safe. The charge is not overcharging. It is that My house has become the place you come to feel secure about what you do everywhere else.
The next morning the tree is dead to the roots, and the answer to Peter's astonishment is about faith and mountains and prayer - said standing beside a tree that made a promise it could not keep.
And prayer is tied to forgiveness immediately. Whenever you stand praying, forgive. The mountain-moving verse does not come without the verse that follows it.
The chapter ends with a legal challenge: by what authority, and who ordained you? And He offers a deal - answer one question and I will answer yours. Was John's baptism from heaven or from men?
Mark lets us hear them work it out, and every word is political. If we say from heaven, He will ask why we did not believe. If we say from men, the crowd will turn. Not one word about what is true.
So they say they do not know, which is a lie. And He declines to hand truth to people who have just demonstrated they will not deal in it.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 12 - The Heir, the Coin, the Greatest Commandment, and Two Small Coins
chapters.title: The Heir, the Coin, the Greatest Commandment, and Two Small Coins
keyNotes: The vineyard is Isaiah 5, and Isaiah's audience already knew the vineyard was Israel. Everyone listening knew what the parable was about before it finished (Mark 12:1, Isaiah 5:1-2).
The details - hedge, winepress, tower - are lifted almost word for word from Isaiah (Mark 12:1).
The tenant system was real: absentee landlords, resented tenants, and long-running disputes over shares (Mark 12:1-2).
The escalating violence against the servants is the history of the prophets, and Mark's readers have just watched one of them beheaded (Mark 12:2-5, 6:27).
"His beloved son" is the phrase the voice from heaven used at the baptism and the transfiguration (Mark 1:11, 9:7, 12:6).
The tenants' reasoning - kill the heir and the inheritance is ours - only makes sense if they know exactly who he is (Mark 12:7).
In Mark the son is killed and then thrown out of the vineyard; He would die outside the city wall (Mark 12:8).
Psalm 118 supplies the answer, and the crowd had been singing that psalm two days earlier (Mark 11:9, 12:10).
"They perceived that he spoke the parable against them" - nobody misunderstood it (Mark 12:12).
Pharisees and Herodians together is the alliance from chapter 3, sent back with a better trap (Mark 3:6, 12:13).
The flattery in verse 14 is entirely accurate, and none of them believe it (Mark 12:14).
The tax was the Roman poll tax, hated because it was the tax of occupation itself (Mark 12:14).
He does not carry the coin. He asks them to produce one - and they do, inside the temple (Mark 12:15-16).
The denarius carried Caesar's image and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus. It was offensive on both counts (Mark 12:16).
"Whose image is this?" uses eikon, the word Genesis uses for what humans are made in. Caesar's image is on the coin; God's image is on the man holding it (Mark 12:16-17, Genesis 1:27).
"And to God the things that are God's" is the larger half of the sentence, and the half they did not ask about (Mark 12:17).
The Sadducees accepted only the five books of Moses, which is why the answer comes from Exodus and not from Daniel or the Psalms (Mark 12:18, 26).
Their riddle is built on levirate marriage, the duty to raise up offspring for a dead brother (Mark 12:19, Deuteronomy 25:5-6).
"You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God" names both halves of the error: bad reading and small expectations (Mark 12:24).
"Like angels in heaven" addresses the marriage question, not the question of whether we know each other (Mark 12:25).
The whole argument turns on a present tense: I am the God of Abraham. Not I was (Mark 12:26-27).
The scribe's question was a live rabbinic debate - the rabbis counted 613 commandments and argued about weight (Mark 12:28).
He answers with the Shema, and Mark alone includes the opening line - Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one (Mark 12:29, Deuteronomy 6:4).
Four faculties are listed where Deuteronomy has three: heart, soul, mind, strength (Mark 12:30).
The scribe agrees, and adds that this is more than all burnt offerings - standing in the temple (Mark 12:33).
"You are not far from God's Kingdom" is warm and unfinished at the same time (Mark 12:34).
Psalm 110 is the most quoted Old Testament passage in the New Testament, and He is the first recorded to use it this way (Mark 12:36).
"The common people heard him gladly" sits immediately before a warning about the religious professionals (Mark 12:37-38).
"Devour widows' houses" probably refers to managing the estates of widows for a fee (Mark 12:40).
And the very next scene is a widow with nothing left. Mark puts them together deliberately (Mark 12:40-42).
Two lepta were the smallest coins in circulation. She could have kept one and nobody would have known (Mark 12:42).
"All that she had to live on" is literally her whole life - bios (Mark 12:44).
He is sitting opposite the treasury watching what people give. That is worth sitting with (Mark 12:41).

intro: Tuesday of the last week, and every faction in Jerusalem takes a turn.

He opens with a parable nobody could possibly misunderstand. A man planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a winepress, built a tower. Anyone who knew Isaiah 5 knew those exact words - and knew that in Isaiah the vineyard is Israel and the owner is God.
So the tenants are the leadership, and the leadership is standing right there.
The servants come one after another and are beaten and shamed and killed, which is the history of the prophets - and Mark's readers have watched John the Baptist beheaded six chapters earlier.

And then: he had one left, his beloved son. That is the phrase the voice from heaven used at the baptism and again on the mountain. Everyone in that courtyard is watching a man tell a story about his own murder, four days before it happens.
And the tenants' reasoning is not confusion. This is the heir - let us kill him and the inheritance will be ours. They know exactly who he is. That is why they kill him.
Verse 12 records how it landed: they perceived that He had spoken the parable against them.

So a trap arrives. Pharisees and Herodians together - an unnatural alliance, since one group hated Roman taxation and the other lived off Roman favour. The flattery they open with is entirely true and entirely insincere.
Is it lawful to pay the poll tax to Caesar? Say yes and the crowd turns on a collaborator. Say no and there is a Roman garrison two hundred yards away.
And He has no coin. He asks them to produce one, and somebody does, inside the temple courts - which is an answer of a kind before anything is said.

Whose image is this? The word is eikon, which is what Genesis uses when it says God made man in His own image. So the reply is layered. Caesar's face is stamped on the coin; give it back to him. God's image is stamped on the man holding it.
And notice which half nobody follows up. Give to Caesar what is Caesar's - fine. And give to God what is God's. That is the enormous half, and no one asks a second question about it.

Then the Sadducees, with a riddle designed to make resurrection look absurd. Seven brothers, one wife, whose is she? They accepted only the five books of Moses, which is why the answer comes from Exodus rather than from Daniel, where resurrection is far plainer.

And the whole argument hangs on a verb tense. At the bush, God says I am the God of Abraham. Not I was. Abraham had been dead four centuries, and God speaks of Himself in the present tense as his God. He is not the God of the dead but of the living.
Then a scribe, and this one is different. He has been listening, he likes the answer, and he asks the real question: which commandment is greatest?
And Mark alone gives the whole Shema - not only love the Lord your God, but the line before it. Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. The confession before the command.

And the scribe agrees and goes further, saying this is more than all burnt offerings - standing in the temple with the smoke going up behind him. And he is told he is not far from the Kingdom, which is warm and unfinished at once.
Then His own question, from Psalm 110, which nobody can answer. And after that, Mark says, nobody dared ask Him anything.

And the last scene places two things together on purpose. First: beware of the scribes who devour widows' houses and make long prayers. Then He sits down opposite the treasury and watches people give.
And a widow puts in two lepta, the smallest coins in circulation. She had two. She could have kept one, and nobody in that courtyard would have known, or cared, or counted.

And He calls the disciples over to make sure they saw it. She has put in more than all of them. They gave out of surplus; she gave out of lack - everything she had to live on. The word is bios. Her whole life.
And immediately after this He walks out of that temple and never returns.

verses.31: The second is like this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”

keyNotes: Herod's temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world. Some of its foundation stones weigh over four hundred tons, and are still there (Mark 13:1).
"Not one stone on another" was fulfilled in AD 70, within the lifetime of many who heard it (Mark 13:2).
The question is asked privately by four men on the Mount of Olives, looking straight across the valley at the building (Mark 13:3).
They ask two things - when, and what sign - and the answer refuses to give a date (Mark 13:4, 32).
The first instruction is not a prediction but a warning: be careful that no one leads you astray (Mark 13:5).
"Birth pains" is a deliberate image: painful, increasing, and ending in life rather than death (Mark 13:8).
Verses 9 to 13 turn from world events to the reader's own life - councils, synagogues, families (Mark 13:9-13).
"The Good News must first be preached to all the nations" is the one thing named as having to happen (Mark 13:10).
"He who endures to the end will be saved" is about endurance, not achievement (Mark 13:13).
The abomination of desolation comes from Daniel, and had already happened once - Antiochus Epiphanes sacrificed a pig on the altar in 167 BC (Mark 13:14, Daniel 11:31).
"Let the reader understand" is Mark speaking directly to us, and it is the only aside like it in the book (Mark 13:14).
The flight instructions are practical and urgent - do not go back for a coat. Eusebius records that the believers did flee Jerusalem before the siege closed (Mark 13:15-16).
"Pray that your flight won't be in the winter" is a small mercy in the middle of a catastrophe (Mark 13:18).
The cosmic language of verses 24 and 25 is drawn from Isaiah and Joel, where it repeatedly describes the fall of nations (Mark 13:24-25, Isaiah 13:10).
"They will see the Son of Man coming in clouds" is Daniel 7 again - and in Daniel the figure comes to God, not to earth (Mark 13:26, Daniel 7:13-14).
The fig tree here is a picture of reading the season, and it is the same tree that was cursed two chapters ago (Mark 11:13, 13:28).

"This generation will not pass away" is the hardest verse in the chapter. Readings include the generation alive in AD 70, the Jewish people as a race, and the generation that sees the final signs. This book does not claim to settle it (Mark 13:30).
"Nor the Son" in verse 32 is startling and was much debated in the early church. Mark records it without softening (Mark 13:32).
The four watches named in verse 35 - evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning - are exactly the four in which the next two chapters happen (Mark 13:35, 14:17, 14:32, 14:72, 15:1).
The last word of the discourse is the word repeated throughout it: watch (Mark 13:37).

intro: They are walking out of the temple, and one of them says what any visitor would say. Teacher, look at these stones.
He was right to be impressed. Herod's temple was one of the wonders of that world, and some of the foundation stones in it weigh more than four hundred tons. They can still be touched.
And the answer is that not one of them will be left on another. Within forty years it was gone: Roman legions took the city in AD 70 and levelled it, and the temple has never been rebuilt.
So four of them ask privately, sitting on the Mount of Olives looking straight across the valley at the building. When? And what is the sign?
And what He does with the question is the pattern of the whole chapter. He does not answer when. He answers how to live in the meantime.
The first thing said is not a prediction but a warning: be careful that nobody leads you astray. That is aimed squarely at people who get excited about prophecy.
Then wars, earthquakes and famines - called the beginning of birth pains. The image is doing real work. Labour pains get worse, not better. And they end in a birth.

Verses 9 to 13 turn personal. Councils. Beatings. Standing before governors. Brother handing over brother. That was not distant history for Mark's first readers, who were being killed in Nero's gardens.
Then verse 14, with a phrase that stops the reader: let the reader understand. That is Mark reaching out of the page, and he does it nowhere else in the book.

The abomination of desolation comes from Daniel, and it had already happened once. In 167 BC Antiochus Epiphanes stopped the sacrifices, set up an altar to Zeus and offered a pig on it. Everyone listening knew the story, and the warning is that it will happen again.

The instructions are practical and urgent. Do not go back into the house. Do not go back for a coat. Pray it is not winter. And history records that when Roman armies approached and there was a lull, the believers left Jerusalem.

Then the cosmic language - sun darkened, moon without light, stars falling. Isaiah uses exactly that language for the fall of Babylon and Ezekiel for Egypt. In the prophets, a sky going dark is how the end of a world order is described.

Then the Son of Man coming in clouds, which is Daniel 7 - and there is something worth noticing there. In Daniel, the one like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days. He goes up, and receives a kingdom.
Then the fig tree, two chapters after a fig tree was cursed - now a lesson about reading the season.

And then verse 30, the hardest verse in the chapter, which should not be made to look simple. This generation will not pass away until all these things happen. Some read generation as the people then alive and point to AD 70. Some read the Greek word as race, meaning the Jewish people will not disappear. Some read it as the generation that sees the final signs begin. Serious readers hold all three. What can be said is that verse 32 stands immediately after: nobody knows the day, not the angels, not the Son.
And then the word the chapter is actually about. Watch, watch, keep alert, watch, watch - four times in the last five verses.

He lists the four watches of the night: evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning. Those are exactly the four in which everything in the next two chapters happens. Supper in the evening. Gethsemane at midnight. Peter at cockcrow. Pilate in the morning.
He tells them to watch. In the garden, they sleep.

keyNotes: The chapter is dated by the Passover, and the leaders want it done before the feast to avoid a riot. They do not get their way (Mark 14:1-2).
Simon the leper is presumably a healed leper, or nobody would be eating in his house (Mark 14:3).
Nard came from the Himalayas. Three hundred denarii is roughly a year's wages for a labourer (Mark 14:3, 5).
She breaks the jar. That is not clumsiness - a sealed alabaster flask was opened by snapping the neck, and it could not be resealed. All of it, at once, or nothing (Mark 14:3).
Anointing was done to kings and to corpses. She does not explain which she meant, and He supplies the answer (Mark 14:8).
"She has done what she could" is one of the gentlest sentences in the Gospel (Mark 14:8).
Judas goes to the chief priests immediately after the grumbling about waste (Mark 14:10).
The man carrying a water jar was a walking signal - that was women's work, and a man doing it would stand out (Mark 14:13).
"One of you will betray me - he who eats with me" echoes Psalm 41, where the betrayer is the friend who shared bread (Mark 14:18, Psalm 41:9).
"Surely not I?" is asked by each of them in turn. None of them looks at Judas (Mark 14:19).
The words over the bread and the cup are spoken during a Passover meal, in the middle of a liturgy that was already about deliverance (Mark 14:22-24).
"My blood of the new covenant" points to Jeremiah 31 and to the blood Moses threw on the people at Sinai (Mark 14:24, Exodus 24:8, Jeremiah 31:31).
"Poured out for many" is the same word used in 10:45 of the ransom (Mark 10:45, 14:24).
The hymn they sang would have been the second half of the Hallel, Psalms 115 to 118 - which ends with the stone the builders rejected (Mark 14:26, Psalm 118:22).
The scattering of the sheep is quoted from Zechariah 13, and He quotes it about Himself (Mark 14:27, Zechariah 13:7).
"After I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee" is a promise of restoration given before the failure happens (Mark 14:28).
Gethsemane means oil press, and it sat among olive trees on the slope opposite the temple (Mark 14:32).
"Greatly troubled and distressed" is unusually strong Greek - the words suggest shuddering horror (Mark 14:33).
"Abba" is the Aramaic word a child used for a father, and Mark keeps it and translates it (Mark 14:36).
"All things are possible to you" - He prays what He taught in 10:27 (Mark 10:27, 14:36).
The cup He asks to be spared is the cup He asked James and John about in chapter 10 (Mark 10:38, 14:36).
He asks three times, and they sleep three times, and Peter - who said he would die first - is the one addressed by his old name, Simon (Mark 14:37-41).
"The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak" is said as an excuse for them, not an accusation (Mark 14:38).
Judas uses the word Rabbi and a kiss - a greeting of affection used as a targeting device (Mark 14:45).
The young man who runs away naked appears in no other Gospel. Many have wondered whether Mark is quietly signing his own book (Mark 14:51-52).
"They all left him, and fled" is the plain summary of every relationship He had (Mark 14:50).
The trial breaks its own law: a capital case at night, on the eve of a feast, with witnesses who do not agree (Mark 14:55-59).
He is silent until asked directly whether He is the Christ - and then answers in two words: I am (Mark 14:61-62).
"I am" is followed immediately by Daniel 7 and Psalm 110. He is convicted on a claim, not on evidence (Mark 14:62-64).
Peter's denials escalate: I do not understand, then a flat denial, then cursing and swearing (Mark 14:68, 70, 71).
A Galilean accent gave him away. He was betrayed by how he spoke (Mark 14:70).
The rooster crows twice, exactly as told - and the last verb in the chapter is wept (Mark 14:72).

intro: Two days before Passover, a woman walks into a dinner and does something that gets her scolded and gets her remembered forever.
Nard came from the Himalayas, the far side of the known world, and three hundred denarii is about a year's wages for a working man. And she breaks the jar.
That detail matters. An alabaster flask was sealed and opened by snapping the neck. Once broken it cannot be closed again. All of it, at once, or nothing.
And the room objects. Why this waste? It could have been sold and given to the poor - which is a perfectly reasonable argument, and it is wrong.
And she is defended with a sentence worth wanting said over one's own life: she has done what she could. Not what she should have. Not what somebody else could have. What she could.
And the next verse is that Judas went to the chief priests. Directly after an argument about money.
Then the upper room, and a man carrying a water jar - which was a signal, because carrying water was women's work and a man doing it stood out. It had all been arranged.

At the table: one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me. Which is Psalm 41, where the betrayer is the friend who shared bread. And notice what they do. Each of them asks, one by one, surely not I? Nobody looks at Judas. Nobody knew.
Then the bread and the cup, inside a Passover meal - a liturgy already about deliverance, blood on doorposts, and God bringing His people out. And He picks it up and points it at Himself.
Then they sing a hymn, which at Passover means the Hallel, Psalms 115 to 118. So the last thing He sang before Gethsemane included the stone the builders rejected.
Then the garden. Gethsemane means oil press - the place where olives are crushed to get at what is inside them.

And Mark uses language here that translators struggle to render. Greatly troubled and distressed is far too polite; the Greek suggests shuddering, appalled horror. This is not a man calmly accepting a plan.
And He falls on the ground. Not kneels. Falls.

And says Abba - the word a child used for a father, kept in Aramaic and then translated. And then: all things are possible to you, which is exactly what He had told the disciples in chapter 10. He believed His own sermon. Take this cup away.
And then: nevertheless, not what I want, but what you want.

And He returns to find them asleep, three times. And Peter is addressed by his old name - Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not watch one hour? The man who a few hours earlier said he would die first.
And even then, what is said about them is a defence rather than an accusation: the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.
Then torches, swords, and a kiss - the sign of affection chosen as the targeting device.
And verse 50, four words long and enormous: they all left him, and fled.

Then the strangest two verses in the Gospel. A young man following in a linen sheet, grabbed by the guards, who wriggles out of it and runs away naked. No other Gospel has it, and many readers have thought it is Mark signing his own book in the corner - and if it is, look at what he chose to record about himself.
Then a trial that breaks its own rules: at night, on the eve of a feast, with witnesses who cannot agree.

And through all of it He says nothing, until the direct question comes - are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And after eight chapters of telling people to keep quiet, the answer is two words. I am. Followed by Daniel 7 and Psalm 110 in a single sentence, which is why the robes get torn.
And downstairs, at a fire in a courtyard, a servant girl looks at a fisherman and says he was with Him. Three rounds later he is cursing and swearing he never knew the man.
His accent gave him away. He was caught by the sound of his own voice.
And then a rooster, for the second time. And the last verb in the chapter is: he wept.

chapters.title: Darkness at Noon, a Curtain Torn, and a Roman Who Understood
keyNotes: The council reconvenes at dawn to make the night verdict legal, and hands Him to Rome because they could not carry out an execution (Mark 15:1).
Pilate's question is political, not theological: are you the King of the Jews? Rome did not care about blasphemy (Mark 15:2).
"So you say" is neither denial nor the answer Pilate wants (Mark 15:2).
The silence in verse 5 makes a Roman governor marvel, and it is Isaiah 53 - he opened not his mouth (Mark 15:5, Isaiah 53:7).
Barabbas means son of the father. He is a murderer and an insurrectionist - a man who did what the crowd wanted a messiah to do (Mark 15:7).
One man goes free and the innocent one takes his place, in the plainest exchange in the Gospels (Mark 15:15).
"For envy" is Pilate's own diagnosis of the chief priests, and Mark records it (Mark 15:10).
A Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone and metal, and men died under it (Mark 15:15).
The whole cohort - up to six hundred men - is called together to mock one prisoner (Mark 15:16).
Purple was imperial. Thorns were a crown. A reed was a sceptre. The mockery is a coronation (Mark 15:17-19).
Simon of Cyrene is named along with his sons, Alexander and Rufus - which only helps if the readers know them. Paul greets a Rufus in Romans 16 (Mark 15:21, Romans 16:13).
He is compelled to carry the crossbeam, which means Yahshua could no longer carry it (Mark 15:21).
Golgotha is Aramaic, and Mark translates it for his readers as he always does (Mark 15:22).
The wine mixed with myrrh was a rough anaesthetic, and He refuses it (Mark 15:23).
"They parted his garments, casting lots" is Psalm 22:18, and Mark reports it without saying so (Mark 15:24, Psalm 22:18).
Mark alone gives the hour: the third hour, nine in the morning (Mark 15:25).
The charge board says THE KING OF THE JEWS. Rome meant it as a warning and it functions as a proclamation (Mark 15:26).
Two robbers, one on the right and one on the left - the seats James and John asked for (Mark 10:37, 15:27).
Verse 28 is absent from the earliest manuscripts. The WEB prints it (Mark 15:28).
"Wagging their heads" is Psalm 22:7. The mockers are quoting the psalm He is about to pray (Mark 15:29, Psalm 22:7).
"He saved others; he cannot save himself" is an accusation that is exactly true, and true in the opposite sense from the one they meant (Mark 15:31).
Darkness from noon to three, over the whole land, at Passover full moon - which is not an eclipse (Mark 15:33).
The cry is Aramaic, and Mark keeps it and translates it. It is the opening line of Psalm 22 (Mark 15:34, Psalm 22:1).
Anyone who knew that psalm knew how it ends - with deliverance and with the nations worshipping (Mark 15:34, Psalm 22:27-31).
The confusion about Elijah works because Eloi and Elias sound alike, and because Malachi had promised Elijah first (Mark 15:35).
The veil torn from top to bottom uses schizo - the same violent verb used when the heavens were torn at the baptism. The Gospel is bracketed by two tearings (Mark 1:10, 15:38).
Top to bottom is a direction. It is not torn by a person (Mark 15:38).
The centurion is the first human being in the whole Gospel to call Him the Son of God - and he is a Gentile, and an executioner, and he says it because of how He died (Mark 1:1, 15:39).
The women are named, and Mark says they had followed and served Him in Galilee. They are the only disciples still present (Mark 15:40-41).
Joseph of Arimathaea is a council member - part of the body that condemned Him - and asking for the body was dangerous (Mark 15:43).
Pilate's surprise that He is already dead is an unintentional witness that He really died (Mark 15:44).
Two women watch where He is laid, which is why they know where to go on Sunday (Mark 15:47).

intro: At dawn the council reconvenes to make the night's verdict legal, and then hands Him to Rome - because they could sentence but could not execute.

And the charge changes on the way. Before the high priest the question was whether He is the Christ. Before Pilate it is whether He is King of the Jews. Blasphemy means nothing to Rome; kingship means everything.
He barely answers, and Pilate marvels - which is Isaiah 53. He opened not his mouth.
Then Barabbas, and there is something in the name. Bar-abbas means son of the father. Pilate puts two men in front of a crowd who both carry that name, and the crowd picks the murderer.

And Barabbas was an insurrectionist who had killed in an uprising - which is to say, exactly the sort of messiah the crowd had been hoping for. Someone who would fight Rome. They chose the version of deliverance they wanted.
And the exchange is the plainest picture of the whole thing. A guilty man walked out of that building free that morning because an innocent one took his cross.

Then the soldiers, and Mark says the whole cohort was called together - possibly six hundred men - to mock one prisoner. What they stage is a coronation. Purple for an emperor. A crown, made of thorns. A reed for a sceptre. Kneeling. Hail, King of the Jews.
They meant it as theatre, and every element of it was true.

Then Simon of Cyrene, pulled out of the crowd - and Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, which is a pointless detail unless the readers know them. Paul greets a Rufus in Romans. A man dragged into someone else's execution, whose family ends up in the church.
And he carries the crossbeam, which tells us that by then Yahshua could not.
The wine mixed with myrrh was a crude painkiller, and He refuses it. He does not go through this half-conscious.
Then Mark writes: crucifying him, they parted his garments, casting lots. He does not stop to say that is Psalm 22. He reports it and moves on, and anyone who knows the psalm feels the floor move.
And the charge board Rome nailed up as a deterrent says THE KING OF THE JEWS. Pilate meant it as an insult, and it is the only true thing anybody wrote down that day.
And two robbers, one on the right and one on the left - which is where James and John wanted to sit.
And the mockery: he saved others, he cannot save himself. Which is exactly the situation. He could not do both.
Then darkness from noon to three. It is Passover, which is full moon, so it is not an eclipse. Whatever it was, the sky went out over that land for three hours.
And out of the dark comes the loudest thing in this Gospel. Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani - kept in Aramaic and then translated, because Mark wants the sound of it heard.

It is Psalm 22, verse 1. Two things should be said carefully. First, the horror of it is real and should not be hurried past. Second, anybody in earshot who knew the psalter knew where that psalm goes. It begins there. It does not end there. It ends with all the ends of the earth remembering and turning to Yahweh.
Then two things happen in two verses.

The curtain in the temple tears, from top to bottom - and the word is schizo, used exactly once before, in chapter 1, when the heavens were torn open at the baptism. The Gospel opens with heaven ripped and closes with the veil ripped. Both times from above. Both times by nobody standing there.
And a Roman centurion - a career executioner who had presumably done this many times - looks at how this man died and says: truly, this man was the Son of God.

Which is the sentence Mark wrote in chapter one, verse one. Fifteen chapters earlier he gave the answer, and then made the reader walk to a hill outside the city to hear a human being say it. Not Peter. Not the twelve. A Gentile soldier, at a cross.

Then the women, who Mark says had followed and served Him all the way from Galilee, and who are the only followers still present. And Joseph of Arimathaea, a member of the council that condemned Him, who goes in and asks for the body - which took real courage.
And two women watch where He is laid, which is how they know where to go on Sunday morning.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 16 - The Stone Already Moved, and a Message With Peter's Name In It
chapters.title: The Stone Already Moved, and a Message With Peter's Name In It
keyNotes: The women wait until the Sabbath is over, then buy spices - which means they expect to find a body (Mark 16:1).
They come at sunrise on the first day of the week (Mark 16:2).
Their only practical worry is the stone, and they set out anyway without a solution to it (Mark 16:3).
"For it was very big" - Mark tells us the problem was real (Mark 16:4).
The stone is already moved when they arrive. Nobody rolls it away to let Him out (Mark 16:4).
The young man in a white robe sits on the right side. Mark does not call him an angel; Matthew does (Mark 16:5).
"You seek Jesus, the Nazarene, who has been crucified" names the death plainly before announcing the resurrection (Mark 16:6).
"He has risen" is passive in form - He was raised. The Father acts (Mark 16:6).
"Behold, the place where they laid him" - the evidence offered is an absence (Mark 16:6).
"Tell his disciples and Peter" singles out by name the man who denied Him three times. That is the whole gospel in two words (Mark 16:7).
"He goes before you into Galilee" repeats the promise made before the failure, in 14:28 (Mark 14:28, 16:7).
Galilee is where it started. They are sent back to the beginning (Mark 1:14, 16:7).
Verse 8 - they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid - is where the two oldest complete manuscripts end the Gospel (Mark 16:8).
An ending there is not incoherent: this is a book where people constantly fail to understand, and it would leave the reader holding the commission (Mark 16:8).

**On the longer ending.** Verses 9 to 20 are absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century; some manuscripts carry a shorter alternative ending instead, and some carry both. Against that, the longer ending is in the vast majority of manuscripts and was known by the second century. This book prints it, as the WEB does, and does not claim the question is settled (Mark 16:9-20).
The vocabulary and style of these verses differ noticeably from the rest of Mark, which is part of the scholarly argument (Mark 16:9-20).
Verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though she had not been named in verse 1, which reads oddly if the same hand wrote both (Mark 16:1, 9).
The longer ending is largely a summary of appearances recorded in Luke and John (Mark 16:9-14).
Three times in six verses somebody refuses to believe an eyewitness. The apostles are not flattered (Mark 16:11, 13, 14).
"Preach the Good News to the whole creation" is the widest commission in any Gospel (Mark 16:15).

**Verses 17 and 18 need care.** Serpents and poison are described as signs that accompanied the apostolic mission, not as practices to attempt. The only snake incident in the New Testament is an accident on Malta. People have died treating this as an instruction; it is not one (Mark 16:18, Acts 28:3-5).
"Received up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God" is Psalm 110 again, where the trial began (Mark 14:62, 16:19).
The last thing the book records is not a farewell but a partnership: the Lord working with them (Mark 16:20).

intro: The Sabbath ends at sundown, and as soon as they can, three women buy spices. Which says exactly what they expected to find.
Nobody goes to that tomb hoping. They are going to finish a burial that had been rushed because the Sabbath was coming.
On the way they have one practical problem, and Mark records the conversation: who will roll away the stone? And then adds - for it was very big.
They had no answer to that, and went anyway.
And when they arrive it is already moved. Which is worth stating plainly: the stone was not rolled away to let Him out. It was rolled away to let them in.
A young man in a white robe, sitting on the right side, tells them not to be amazed - which is rather like telling someone not to breathe.

And then: you are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. The death is named, not softened, and then - He has risen. He is not here. Look at the place where they laid him. The evidence offered is an empty shelf.
And then verse 7. Go, tell his disciples - and Peter.
And Peter. Why say that? Everyone knew Peter was a disciple; he is the first one named in the book.

Because Peter did not know it any more. The last time he appears he is standing by a fire swearing he had never met the man, and then a rooster crows and he goes outside and breaks. As far as Peter was concerned, he had resigned.
And the first message out of the empty tomb has his name in it, specifically and separately, so there is no chance of assuming he is not included.
And go to Galilee - where it all started in chapter 1. They are sent back to the beginning to begin again.
And then verse 8. They went out and fled, trembling and astonished, and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
And that is where the two oldest complete copies of this Gospel stop.

The longer ending is printed here, and readers should know what it is. Verses 9 to 20 are missing from the oldest manuscripts. Some copies carry a different, shorter ending instead; some carry both. On the other side, the vast majority of manuscripts do have it, and it was being quoted in the second century.

The question is not settled, and this book does not claim to settle it. What can be said is that nothing in these verses teaches anything unavailable elsewhere - the appearances are in Luke and John, and the commission is in Matthew.

Except for two lines, which need dealing with plainly. Verses 17 and 18 mention taking up serpents and drinking deadly things. There are churches that handle venomous snakes on the strength of that verse, and people have died.

Read as written, these are described as things that would accompany believers, not as instructions to go and do. And the one occasion anybody in the New Testament picks up a snake, it is Paul on Malta, gathering firewood, entirely by accident. Nobody in Scripture tests God on purpose.
And the last verse: He was taken up, and sat down at the right hand of God - which is Psalm 110, the verse He was condemned for quoting.
And they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them.
Which is how this book ends: not with a farewell but with a partnership. He is not on the page any more. He is out there, with them, working.

Sixteen chapters. A Gospel that started at a run and never slowed, that gave the answer in verse one and made the reader walk to a cross to hear a human being say it. And it ends with an empty tomb, a message with a failed man's name in it, and a Lord who went on ahead.
